items.title: People once needed the pope’s permission to put butter in this beloved Christmas bread
items.summary:
If you’ve never had stollen bread , picture a dense, sweet, doughy loaf filled with dried fruit, nuts, and occasionally a roll of sweet marzipan or almond paste, then flavored with warm spices, and covered in a generous layer of powdered sugar. With all those rich, festive flavors packed into one dish, it’s easy to see why stollen became well-loved Christmas treat.

But stollen wasn’t always such a decadent holiday dessert. 

Sure, it’s been a German Christmas tradition for centuries , with the earliest documented mention dating to 1474 in Dresden . But at that time, the recipe was about as far from today’s version as you could imagine.

Bakers had to get creative during Advent 

Stollen was originally a simple fasting bread, made only with flour, yeast, and water. That’s because Advent was a period of fasting in Catholic Germany. During which the Catholic Church restricted the use of ingredients including butter and milk. Bakers could use oil instead, but the resulting loaf was a pretty austere version of what would eventually become a Christmas favorite.

Still, people wanted something more indulgent. According to the traditional story, Saxon rulers Ernst and Albrecht decided to do something about it. By the late 15th century, they had asked the pope to lift the restriction on butter so bakers could make richer stollen during Advent.

Behold, a merciful Butterbrief 

The pope initially refused, but the request eventually succeeded. Around 1490, Pope Innocent VIII issued a decree known as the Butterbrief , or “Butter Letter,” allowing bakers in Saxony to use butter in…
items.t: People once needed the pope’s permission to put butter in this beloved Christmas bread

items.title: Psychologist shares an easy way to reconnect with old friends without making things awkward
items.summary:
Some friendships slip away, not because it’s anyone’s fault, but because life changes . People get new jobs, pick up new hobbies and interests, and go through big family changes, which shuffle the deck of who we come into contact with day to day.

Then, one day, you wake up and realize that you haven’t seen a good friend in 6 months. At this point, you feel uncomfortable reaching out because they could be angry with you for ignoring them. Or you fear they’ve forgotten about you because you’re not in regular contact. Picking up the phone feels uncomfortable because what if they don’t pick up, or you don’t know what to say?

Psychologist Adam Grant has an easy, science-backed way to reach out to people you’ve fallen out of touch with that makes both parties comfortable: send a voice text. Grant is an organizational psychologist, bestselling author, podcast host, and the author of Vibe: The Secrets of Strong Connections in a Lonely World .

How to reconnect with old friends 

“One of the I think the easiest things you can do if you want to reconnect with somebody that you’ve lost touch with is record a voice note and send it to them,” Grant told Rich Roll on The Rich Roll Podcast. “You just record a little message that says, ‘Hey, I know it’s been a while. I miss you. I’ve been thinking of you. Here’s why I appreciate the role you’ve played in my life. Here’s an article I read that I thought you would love. I just watched a movie that I think would be right up your alley. Would love to catch up and then see how they reply.” 

Grand adds that a voice text is much more…
items.t: Psychologist shares an easy way to reconnect with old friends without making things awkward

items.title: A Sears customer could order a house by mail. In some attics, the lumber still has its address.
items.summary:
Not so long ago, flipping through a Sears Catalog was the modern version of home shopping. Even back then, someone could pick out a house and order the materials to build it. The supplies would arrive by train, along with instructions for putting it all together.

Customers could choose anything from a modest bungalow to a spacious family home , and many of those houses are still standing today. While some have changed considerably over the years, they may contain clues to their origins. One is a series of letters and numbers stamped on pieces of wood that have been holding the house together for decades.

Sears Catalog Modern Home No. 145. Photo Credit: Sears, Roebuck & Co./ Wikimedia Commons 

When Americans ordered their homes from Sears 

In 1908, according to the Sears Archives , Sears, Roebuck and Co. published its first catalog dedicated to houses. The Book of Modern Homes and Building Plans featured 22 designs ranging in price from $650 to $2,500.

Customers could browse illustrations of the houses and examine their floor plans before deciding which one to purchase. Sears eventually began offering mortgages, too.

“The Hazelton” model No. C2025 from the Sears catalog, 1916. Photo Credit: Sears, Roebuck & Co./ Wikimedia Commons 

Ordering the house didn’t mean that a fully assembled building would arrive at the individual’s property. The company shipped building materials that the buyer or a hired builder would then use to construct the home.

According to the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond , the materials arrived by rail at a nearby depot, leaving customers…
items.t: A Sears customer could order a house by mail. In some attics, the lumber still has its address.

items.title: Janis Ian wrote about being 17. The letters that came back told her who had been listening.
items.summary:
“I learned the truth at seventeen, that love was meant for beauty queens…” 

Janis Ian’s 1975 folk-pop hit “At Seventeen” has resonated with lonely teens for generations. The simple composition, just a girl and her guitar, reinforces the lyrics lamenting how the pretty and popular win the game of love, while the ugly ducklings with “ravaged faces” stay at home “inventing lovers on the phone.” 

It’s a tale as old as time, but Ian told it in a way that felt personal to every teen (and even former teen) who relates to it. Ian herself has said the song is about “opening up to your worst fears about yourself and laying them on the table,” an acknowledgement so many teens are desperate for.

#LifeInSongs 
Teen

Nirvana? too obvious
Teenager in love Dion? too poppy

Janis Ian At 17 just freakin right! pic.twitter.com/LHXbgExpj9 

— rvd74 (@rvd74) September 16, 2022 

She wrote the song at 23 

Ian was well past teen angst when she wrote “At Seventeen.” The song was inspired by her own experiences, though the opening line came from an article she read by a woman who had expected her life to be perfect after her debutante ball. “I learned the truth at 18,” the article began. Ian changed the age to 17 for the rhythm and started writing her hit song about feeling like an ugly duckling.

“It took three months to write, because it was scary,” Ian shared in The Guardian in 2018. “This was the mid-70s, before confessional songs, and I’d never been that honest about feeling ugly and never being asked out. I kept picking it up and putting it down, saying: ‘I can’t do this.’ In the…
items.t: Janis Ian wrote about being 17. The letters that came back told her who had been listening.

items.title: Making Peace With a Himalayan ‘Ghost’
items.summary:
L ast winter, Deachen Chuskit took her cows to graze in the upper Himalayan desert of Ladakh. The snow had covered the pasturelands nearby, forcing her and other villagers to take their livestock farther from their village, Saspotse, for grazing. When she returned for the animals in the evening, she found they were agitated.  

“One of my cows had been killed by a snow leopard,” she says. “I cried for my cow, and then for my loss.”  

Goats grazing along the bank of a creek in Ladakh. Credit: Minh Cong Pham / Shutterstock 
 Twenty years ago, villagers might have retaliated by killing the snow leopard, which is listed as vulnerable on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list of threatened species. “These happened often when I was young,” says Tsewang Namgail, who heads the Ladakh-based Snow Leopard Conservancy – India Trust (SLC-IT). “Growing up in a remote Ladakhi village I used to herd our sheep and goats. My favorite was a goat we’d named Karmo, the white one. One night, a snow leopard killed her. I was very young but remember feeling bad for days, months, actually. From then on, I thought of snow leopards as ugly pests.”  

Deachen Chuskit. Courtesy of Geetanjali Krishna 
 But this was before he had seen a snow leopard in the wild. Such sightings are rare because these big cats, called the ghosts of the mountains, are elusive and superbly camouflaged in the snowy terrain. “Years later, I was doing some field research in Ladakh, and happened to see the silhouettes of two sub-adult snow leopards, barely 15 meters away from me,” he recalls. “It was…
items.t: Making Peace With a Himalayan ‘Ghost’

items.title: Two people had a conversation. Researchers asked each when they secretly wanted it to end.
items.summary:
If you’ve ever found yourself wondering whether a conversation has gone on long enough, there’s a decent chance the person you’re talking to is wondering the same thing.

The problem is, neither of you may realize it.

A 2021 study found that people often struggle to end conversations at the moment they actually want them to end. And this isn’t just a problem between strangers. It can happen even when we’re talking to people we know well.

Researchers Adam Mastroianni, Daniel Gilbert, Gus Cooney, and Timothy Wilson conducted two studies of a total of 932 conversations to investigate what happens when people want conversations to end.

Even people we know can miss the signal 

Friends chatting over coffee and smiling. Canva 

In the first study, 806 people reported on a recent conversation with a friend, family member, or romantic partner. The researchers asked when they had wanted the conversation to end and when they thought the other person had wanted it to end.

Often, the conversation didn’t end when either partner wanted it to. It was also common for partners to think the other person wanted to keep talking longer than they did.

So the researchers designed a second study that let them see what was happening from both sides.

Strangers offered striking results 

Strangers talking in a cafe. Canva 

For the second experiment, researchers brought 252 strangers into a lab and paired them up. Each pair was told to talk about whatever they wanted for as little or as much time as they liked, as long as the conversation lasted more than one minute and less than 45 minutes.…
items.t: Two people had a conversation. Researchers asked each when they secretly wanted it to end.

items.title: Berlin is putting AI cameras on its streets. An artist made a brilliant shirt to outsmart it.
items.summary:
In photos and video Simon Weckert shot outside Berlin’s Kottbusser Tor subway station, a computer program draws a green box around each pedestrian and labels it “person.” Weckert, standing among them, gets no box at all.

The difference is his shirt , a loose, short-sleeve button-down covered in blurry, saturated blobs of color. He calls it Digital Camouflage.

Weckert is the Berlin artist who went viral in 2020 for pulling 99 smartphones through the city in a wagon, which made Google Maps show traffic jams on nearly empty streets. 

His new target is the AI surveillance Berlin police have brought to Kottbusser Tor, a busy transit hub in the Kreuzberg district.

Police began installing about 30 cameras there in late August. According to the Berliner Kurier , it’s the first time Berlin has put a public space outside its transit system under permanent video surveillance. Software watches the live feeds and alerts officers when it spots behavior it’s built to flag, mainly fights and other emergencies, the German news agency dpa reported .

Weckert’s concern is who else gets flagged because systems like this can pick out someone lying on the ground, he told 404 Media , and “homeless people could be detected and police get triggered.”

The shirt exploits how detectors learn. They’re trained on millions of example images, so what they actually recognize is a statistical pattern, not a human being. “A ‘person,’ for the machine, is a bundle of visual statistics,” Weckert told Dezeen.

He built the print against YOLO , a free and widely used object-detection program. Software…
items.t: Berlin is putting AI cameras on its streets. An artist made a brilliant shirt to outsmart it.

items.title: Almond milk is about 800 years old, and medieval cooks had a clever reason to make it
items.summary:
If you’ve ever ordered an almond milk latte, odds are you weren’t picturing yourself participating in a culinary tradition that goes back to the Middle Ages .

But almond milk isn’t a modern invention created for the age of newly discovered dietary restrictions and lactose aversion. People in medieval Europe were making and cooking with it centuries ago, and they had a particularly practical reason for doing so. Not to mention a religiously motivated one. 

When dairy was off the menu, almonds came to the rescue 

During Christian fasting periods , particularly Lent, medieval rules prohibited the consumption of certain animal products, including dairy, for a good chunk of the year. For cooks accustomed to making rich dishes with milk, butter, and eggs, that created a culinary conundrum. 

A medieval stained glass panel from Canterbury Cathedral, c. 1175 – c. 1180, depicting the Parable of the Sower, a biblical narrative. Wikipedia 

Thankfully, almond milk, which had already been well established in Middle Eastern cuisine , offered a solution .

For one, it was f airly simple to make . Grind almonds, mix them with water, and strain the resulting liquid. Done. And, once made, almond milk could do milk’s job of thickening sauces, soups, stews, and desserts. Obviously, this chameleonic quality could provide the perfect culinary loophole. A 14th-century German cookbook called Das Buch von guter Speise , for example, features several Lenten fasting recipes that utilize chicken or fish cooked in thick almond milk as a dairy substitute. Other medieval recipes used almond milk…
items.t: Almond milk is about 800 years old, and medieval cooks had a clever reason to make it

items.title: High tea is meant to be shared. Doing it alone in London taught me a profound life lesson.
items.summary:
“Just one?” This is a question I get asked often, and I’m happy to answer with variations of yes. “That’s right. You got it. One indeed!” It has never bothered me, and on the contrary, it fills me with a tiny sense of self-actualized pride. Dinners, movies , concerts. I unequivocally prefer to be on my own, voyeuristically eavesdropping on other people’s lives.

To be clear, I like other people’s company in spurts and love, for lack of a better word, “collecting” people as I move through life. But solitude , for the most part, fits best. This is especially true when it comes to traveling. Swiping that train card, with no one watching my clock, fills me with pure glee. But on a recent trip to my favorite city, London, I hit a bit of a snag.

High tea at The Kensington, Photo byCecily Knobler 

Just one? 

After joyously getting lost in two red-and-gold-swathed parks, I decided it was time for high tea. So I returned to The Kensington Hotel (where I was staying) and made a reservation for that day at 4:00 p.m. “Just you, Ms. Knobler?” the kind man with the top hat asked at the desk. “If that changes,” I said with a wink, “I’ll let you know.”

Clad in a black cashmere sweater and a pink and black checkered miniskirt, I checked in with the hosts right on time. They showed me around the various delicate rooms, so that I could pick my spot. Would it be the library, surrounded by leather-bound books by Dickens? Near a fireplace lightly decorated with silver Christmas tinsel? I settled on a seat by a bay window, as the last drops of the sun were squeezed into the space. 

But I…
items.t: High tea is meant to be shared. Doing it alone in London taught me a profound life lesson.

items.title: Mr. Feeny saved his goodbye for an empty classroom. William Daniels remembered filming it.
items.summary:
Mr. Feeny, the iconic teacher and principal at the heart of Boy Meets World , was brought to life and made unforgettable by the acting talents of William Daniels. However, it almost didn’t happen.

Daniels famously quit the show after the very first table read of the pilot script. He had too much respect for “the underpaid, underappreciated teachers of this country to portray one of them a fool,” per Daniels’ own biography . He didn’t want to play a goofball educator who was only there for laughs.

Luckily, the role was rewritten, Daniels returned to the cast , and the rest is history. But of all the heartfelt, emotional, and wise moments Daniels’ brought us as Feeny, one is permanently etched into the hearts of anyone who grew up watching the show.

Mr. Feeny’s iconic farewell 

The series finale of Boy Meets World , “Brave New World: Part 2”, aired in 2000; well over 20 years ago now.

But many Millennials can still remember watching the show’s final scene as if it were yesterday.

Mr. Feeny gathers in the classroom with his students Cory, Topanga, Shawn, and Eric one final time. As the seventh season of the show comes to a close, each of the main protagonists is preparing to finally leave the nest. They’ll all be moving away from Philadelphia for the first time, finally leaving Feeny behind. 

He leaves them with parting words of advice: “Believe in yourselves. Dream. Try. Do good.” Topanga, ever the A-plus student, asks if he means “Do well.” 

“No, I mean ‘do good’,” he responds.

Tearful goodbyes ensue, and the kids go on their way out into the big world.

items.t: Mr. Feeny saved his goodbye for an empty classroom. William Daniels remembered filming it.

items.title: Mom started baking Girl Scouts cookies her allergic daughter could eat. Now she’s raised $30 million.
items.summary:
A new Girl Scout cookie , on sale in January, started with a snack that sent a baby to the emergency room .

The baby was Denise Woodard’s daughter, Vivienne, and the snack had just two ingredients, peanuts and corn. Vivienne turned out to be allergic to corn, along with eggs, tree nuts and bananas.

Woodard, then a sales executive at Coca-Cola, immediately pictured her daughter growing up as the “allergy kid” with the “allergy snacks,” she told Snack Food & Wholesale Bakery magazine. The allergy-friendly options in stores didn’t impress her, so she started baking her own cookies, free of the most common allergens.

View this post on Instagram 

She launched Partake in 2016, selling cookies store by store out of her car, and eventually left Coca-Cola to run it. Keeping it afloat took her 401(k) and then her engagement ring.

At least 86 investors turned her down, Woodard told CBS News in 2022. “I took it pretty personal,” she said.

View this post on Instagram 

The first yes came in 2019 from Marcy Venture Partners, the fund Jay-Z co-founded, which led a $1 million round. According to Partake , that made Woodard the first Black woman to publicly raise $1 million for a packaged food startup.

That same year, when Partake had exactly one other employee, Woodard told her they were going to make a Girl Scout cookie one day.

“I think she thought I had lost the plot!” Woodard told TODAY .

Rihanna and H.E.R. later invested, and Partake’s cookies are now sold in thousands of stores. In September, the Girl Scouts announced Girl Scout Sparkables, their first allergy-friendly…
items.t: Mom started baking Girl Scouts cookies her allergic daughter could eat. Now she’s raised $30 million.

items.title: The Portlanders Turning Rescued Food Into Restaurant-Quality Meals
items.summary:
I t’s a Tuesday morning in early October and chef Bradley Cohen, 49, is trying to improvise a meal from a hotel pan full of pork loins. He pulls a crate of fresh kale and zucchini from the walk-in, noting the date it was brought in (Sunday), and says he’ll probably blanch the veggies.  

“The problem is not that there’s not enough food — it’s just in the wrong places,” he says. 

Bradley Cohen is among the chefs who turn donated ingredients into restaurant-worthy meals for Urban Gleaners. Credit: Hannah Wallace 
 He checks out the spices and other ingredients that have appeared in the pantry since his last visit to this centrally located kitchen and grows animated when he finds a container of gochujang, a savory-spicy fermented condiment popular in Korean cooking. “I always get excited when I find this because it adds umami,” he says. He decides on the spot that he’ll make a gochujang-veggie bouillon braising sauce for the pork loins. To complete the meal, he’ll make some macaroni, tossed in butter, garlic powder and paprika. 

This madcap cooking challenge isn’t for Chopped . It’s for a Portland, Oregon-based gleaning organization. Urban Gleaners is a 20-year-old nonprofit that rescues food before it goes into the waste stream — and helps feed hungry Portlanders.  

Gleaning, the practice of collecting leftover crops from farmers’ fields or orchards, is nothing new: There are references to gleaning in the Bible, and it was widely employed by the rural poor in the 16th and 17th centuries. And today, there are hundreds of gleaning nonprofits across the U.S. But Urban…
items.t: The Portlanders Turning Rescued Food Into Restaurant-Quality Meals

items.title: What We’re Reading: Building a Walkable City From Scratch
items.summary:
Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. 

City of tomorrow

At first glance, the sky seems to be the limit for Utah City, a new community in one of Utah’s fastest-growing cities, with the developer citing the cost of constructing high rises as the only constraint. The development checks all the boxes for the kind of sustainable, pedestrian-first urban living we often cover at RTBC: high density, walkability, green spaces, convenient transit options. And the project is ambitious , expected to be finished in 15 to 20 years. 

But Utah City faces heavy scrutiny, as Grist and the Salt Lake Tribune report in a story shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby. Though one new resident describes it as “rad” and “vibey,” members of the local city council call it a “gamble,” expressing skepticism that such a community makes sense in a place full of freeways and single-family homes. As one council member put it: “Walkability I don’t care about. [It] forces a lifestyle the average person isn’t living. Most people drive a car.” 

Becca says: 
 If you build it, will they come? This is a fascinating look at a dense, transit-centered development that seems great on paper but may not be compatible with local desires.

items.title: The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool
items.summary:
A s a taxi driver, Juan Barbosa should in theory be one of the strongest opponents of a crackdown on cars. But, puffing on a cigarette beside his vehicle on a sultry August afternoon, the inhabitant of Pontevedra, Spain, admits that he finds himself in something of an existential crisis. 

“As a driver, I suffer,” says Barbosa, who has been ferrying passengers around the northwestern city for two decades. “We can’t enter certain areas unless we have a customer or a booking. We have to take longer routes. But as a pedestrian, life is better. I enjoy it when there are fewer vehicles around.” 

Post-pandemic, pedestrian-first urban planning is now all the rage, from 15-minute cities to low-traffic zones and the rise of soft mobility ( human-powered or low-emission electric transport). But Pontevedra, which is home to 85,000 people in the city and just under a million in the province, was way ahead of the curve. It technically began its war on cars last century. (In 1999, to be precise.) 

The urban transformation of Pontevedra was carried out gradually, over the course of several years. Credit: Peter Yeung 
 Today Pontevedra, which fittingly is located on one of the world-famous Camino de Santiago pilgrimage routes , is considered perhaps the greatest example in the world when it comes to getting rid of cars. Every year, delegations of mayors, professors and city planners make their own pilgrimage to learn about this great vanishing act. 

“Pontevedra is an influential example and something we speak of often,” says Mark Nieuwenhuijsen , director of the urban planning,…
items.t: The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool
